ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was granted by the University of Bristol Human Research Ethics Committee (Ref: 2020-7982-7929).
In a pre-registered online experiment, participants completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism, and undertook a judgement bias task.

These translational tasks were originally developed for use with animals, on the basis of findings from human psychology that people with mood disorders, or in induced negative affective states, interpreted ambiguous words, phrases, facial expressions, and future scenarios more negatively (e.g. Eysenck et al., 1991; Joormann & Gotlib, 2006; Mathews et al., 1989; Park et al., 2016; Wright & Bower, 1992). In Harding et al.'s (2004) original animal judgement bias task, rats were trained to press a lever when they heard a tone associated with a food reward, and to refrain from pressing the lever when they heard a different tone to avoid a punishment (white noise).

table.text: Conversely, if the participant had similar reaction time profiles for both responses but responded 'pessimistically' more often, this would be reflected by a negative drift rate (with drift rate = 0 reflecting no drift towards either boundary) and suggest that the negative bias was generated during the decision-making process.

For example, Aylward et al. (2020) used a two-tone discrimination task in which participants had to press one key when a certain tone played to receive a high reward of £4 and had to press another key when a different tone played to receive a low reward of £1.

table.text: During testing, participants were also presented with an intermediate ambiguous tone on some trials, and their responses to this ambiguous tone were investigated.

In the task, participants had to decide whether to make the 'optimistic' response (the response associated with receiving a high reward) or the 'pessimistic' response (the response associated with receiving a low reward) when shown ambiguous visual stimuli.
Participants provided informed consent via an online consent form.
Participants were recruited and reimbursed for their time via Prolific (www.prolific.com).
table.formatted: Participants were recruited and reimbursed for their time via Prolific (<ref type="url" target="www.prolific.com">www.prolific.com</ref>).

table.text: The inclusion criteria were: (1) individuals over 18 years old, (2) individuals who currently lived in the UK, and (3) individuals who selected 'United Kingdom' as their nationality on Prolific.
To encourage engagement with the task, participants were told that they had a chance to earn the 20p bonus depending on whether they responded correctly on one trial selected at random.

To ensure that participants were attending to the possible trial outcomes, they were also told that for every 100 people that completed the task, the best performing participant would receive an extra bonus of £10.

We recruited 540 participants in total, based on a 93% completion rate observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al. (2022). 20 participants withdrew from the study, and data from a further 4 participants were excluded due to poor performance in the task (responding incorrectly on 50% or more of either of the unambiguous stimuli trials).

table.text: All participants completed the study in a fixed order: consent form, judgement bias task (see below), LOT-R questionnaire, PHQ-8 questionnaire, GAD-7 questionnaire, demographics questionnaire.
Participants were instructed to ensure that they were sat upright, 60cm from the screen and that their screen was level.
To ensure that the stimuli appeared correctly, participants were required to calibrate their screen using Gorilla's screen calibration function.
Participants were told that the aim of the task was to earn as much money as possible.
Prior to each testing block, participants completed a training block of 20 trials using only the unambiguous stimuli.
During testing participants were also presented with ambiguous patches which were only slightly tilted to the left or right.
In addition, data from 4 participants were excluded due to poor performance in the task (responding incorrectly on 50% or more of either of the unambiguous stimuli trials).

Sex was a significant predictor of Optimistic Responses (LRT = 36.474, p < 0.001); post-hoc analysis revealed that male participants had significantly higher Optimistic Responses than females (male mean: 0.63, female mean: 0.56; z = 5.961, p < 0.001, Figure 4).

table.text: Using a large-scale preregistered online experiment where participants completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism, and undertook a judgement bias task, we confirmed that selfreported negative affect is associated with negative judgement biases during decision-making under ambiguity; individuals who reported higher anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-8) scores made a significantly lower proportion of 'optimistic' responses when faced with ambiguous stimuli in the judgement bias task.
Male participants were also significantly more 'optimistic' than females in the task, a finding not observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al.'s (2022) study.
A) Participants were required to classify Gabor patches as tilted to the left or right of vertical.
Each participant completed 240 trials in total with the four stimuli equally represented. n=516.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To determine the target sample size, we used G*Power (v3.1.9.7, Faul et al., 2007) to conduct a power calculation. The power calculation was based on a finding from a similar study (Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022), where a significant correlation of r=-0.13 was observed between the proportion of 'optimistic' responses to ambiguous stimuli in a decision-making task and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores. The calculation used p < 0.05 and 90% power giving a target sample size of 503 participants. We recruited 540 participants in total, based on a 93% completion rate observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al. (2022). 20 participants withdrew from the study, and data from a further 4 participants were excluded due to poor performance in the task (responding incorrectly on 50% or more of either of the unambiguous stimuli trials). This gave a final sample size of 516 (273 female; 236 male; 4 other; 3 prefer not to say; aged 18-73; median age = 36 years). Due to the low number of participants reporting their sex as 'other' or 'prefer not to say', statistical comparisons are only made between participants reporting their sex as 'male' or 'female'. Data from participants reporting their sex as 'other' or 'prefer not to say' are still included in the analyses.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: The effects of negative trait affect on decision-making under ambiguity
table.research_questions:
We hypothesise that negative trait affect will be associated with pessimistic decisions to ambiguous stimuli:

1) We predict a negative correlation between pessimism scores (measured using the LOT-R) and the proportion of optimistic responses made for the ambiguous stimuli.

2) We predict a negative correlation between anxiety symptom scores (measured using the GAD-7) and the proportion of optimistic responses made for the ambiguous stimuli.

3) We predict a negative correlation between depression symptom scores (measured using the PHQ-8) and the proportion of optimistic responses made for the ambiguous stimuli.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: We will run an online experiment using Gorilla (https://gorilla.sc/). Participants will be recruited and reimbursed for their time via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/). The inclusion criteria are individuals over 18 years old who live in the UK. The whole experiment should take around 20 minutes to complete and participants will be paid £1.80 for their time plus a bonus of 20p. To encourage engagement with the task participants will be told that they have a chance to earn the 20p bonus depending on whether they respond correctly on one trial selected at random. All participants will receive the 20p bonus regardless of performance. To ensure that participants are attending to the possible trial outcomes, they will be told that for every 100 people that complete the task, the best performing participant will receive an extra bonus of £10.
table.sample_size:
Our target sample size is 503 participants. We will recruit 540 participants, assuming that not all participants will complete the whole study. This is based on the 93% completion rate (7% non-completion) observed in a similar study (Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2020).

table.sample_size_rationale:
We used G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) to conduct a power calculation. The power calculation was based on a finding from a similar study (Daniel- Watanabe et al., 2020), where a correlation of r=-0.13 was observed between the proportion of optimistic responses to  ambiguous stimuli in a decision-making task and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores. The calculation used p < 0.05 and 90% power.


Daniel-Watanabe, L., McLaughlin, M., Gormley, S., & Robinson, O. (2020). Association Between a Directly Translated Cognitive Measure of Negative Bias and Self-reported Psychiatric Symptoms. Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience And Neuroimaging. doi: 10.1016/j.bpsc.2020.02.010
Faul, F., Erdfelder, E., Lang, A., & Buchner, A. (2007). G*Power 3: A flexible statistical power analysis program for the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences. Behavior Research Methods, 39(2), 175-191. doi: 10.3758/bf03193146
table.measured_variables:
Participants will complete several questionnaires as well as a decision-making task. The task will involve classifying Gabor patch images of various orientations as leaning to the left or the right by making keyboard press responses (‘z’ for left, ‘m’ for right). There will be two unambiguous stimuli (-3.2 and 3.2 degrees from vertical) and two ambiguous stimuli (-0.05 and 0.05 degrees from vertical). Correct responses will be rewarded with either a high reward (£4) or low reward (£1) depending on the Gabor patch orientation (left or right) and participants will receive £0 for an incorrect response. Participants will be told that the aim of the experiment is to win as much money as possible.  

The high/low reward direction will be counterbalanced within a participant to account for any directional bias i.e. where a participant is predisposed to select either the left or right key, regardless of the stimulus. Participants will therefore complete 2 testing blocks, one where left-leaning patches are rewarded with £4 and one where left-leaning patches are rewarded with £1 (and vice versa for right-leaning patches). Both testing blocks will consist of 120 trials with all four stimuli equally represented across testing trials in a fixed random order. Prior to each testing block, participants will complete a training block of 20 trials using only the unambiguous stimuli. Only data from the testing blocks will be included in the analysis. 

The key outcome of interest is the proportion of optimistic responses for the ambiguous stimuli. Here we define an optimistic response as the response associated with the high-reward (£4) direction. 

Variables measured from questionnaires:
•	Pessimism score, measured using the Revised Life Orientation Test (LOT-R)
•	Anxiety symptoms score, measured using the Generalised Anxiety Disorder Assessment (GAD-7) 
•	Depression symptoms score, measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire eight item depression measure (PHQ-8)
•	Sex, options are Male, Female, Prefer not to say, Other (please specify)
•	Age, options from 18 to 81+ years old

Variables measured for each trial of the decision-making task:
•	Response – which key (‘z’ or ‘m’) has been pressed 
•	Reaction time – time between stimulus presentation and key press response
table.indices: The proportion of optimistic responses will be combined across both ambiguous stimuli to give each participant a single 'proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli' variable.
table.statistical_tests:
To determine whether there is an association between negative trait affect and pessimistic decisions to ambiguous stimuli, we will use a generalised linear model (GLM).  The dependent variable will be the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli. The independent variables included in the model will be pessimism (LOT-R) score, anxiety (GAD-7) score, depression (PHQ-8) score, sex and age. We hypothesise a negative association between pessimism scores/anxiety scores/depression scores and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli, therefore for each of these variables a negative beta coefficient and p < 0.05 will be treated as a significant result that confirms the corresponding hypothesis.

As we predict a degree of association between the independent variables related to negative trait affect (LOT-R, GAD-7 and PHQ-8 scores), we will also separately test for correlations between:

•	Pessimism (LOT-R) scores and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli
•	Anxiety (GAD-7) scores and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli
•	Depression (PHQ-8) scores and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli

This will be done using three separate GLMs, where the questionnaire score is the independent variable and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli is the dependent variable. For each GLM, a negative beta coefficient and p < 0.05 will be treated as a significant result that confirms the corresponding hypothesis.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Data from participants who do not complete the whole experiment will be excluded. Data from participants who do not sufficiently complete the task, i.e. respond correctly on less than 50% of the unambiguous trials, will be excluded. Data from trials where the reaction times are too short (<200ms) or too long (>2000ms) will be excluded from the analysis.
table.exploratory_analyses: To allow us to investigate how negative trait affect influences the decision-making process at the individual level, we will apply drift-diffusion modelling to the data.

Responses to the two ambiguous stimuli (Ambiguous Negative and Ambiguous Positive) were compared using a paired-samples t-test, the assumptions of which were met; a Shapiro-Wilk test indicated that the difference scores did not deviate from normality (W = 0.998, p = 0.777) supported by visual inspection of the histogram and Q-Q plots.
A statistically significant difference was observed (t(515) = -2.15, p = 0.032) albeit with a very small effect size (mean difference = -0.008; Cohen's dz = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.18, -0.01]).

No significant difference in 'optimistic' responses between the Ambiguous Negative and Ambiguous Positive stimuli was found in post-hoc comparisons of our trial-level analysis (z = 2.496, p = 0.055; see supplementary material).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "The calculation used p < 0.05 and 90% power giving a target sample size of 503 participants."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. table.expanded: Responses to the two ambiguous stimuli (Ambiguous Negative and Ambiguous Positive) were compared using a paired-samples t-test, the assumptions of which were met; a Shapiro-Wilk test indicated that the difference scores did not deviate from normality (W = 0.998, p = 0.777) supported by visual inspection of the histogram and Q-Q plots.

No significant difference in 'optimistic' responses between the Ambiguous Negative and Ambiguous Positive stimuli was found in post-hoc comparisons of our trial-level analysis (z = 2.496, p = 0.055; see supplementary material).
The effects of anxiety (LRT = 1.031, p = 0.310), depression (LRT = 0.493, p = 0.483), and pessimism (LRT = 0.153, p = 0.696) on Optimistic Responses were not significant in this model.

data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 50 files: 32 data, 17 code, 1 documentation.
-  We found 26 tabular data files and extracted 388 columns from 25 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex34), plus 1 collection-level file (README/ro-crate metadata).
-  1 tabular data file could not be read because it was not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass `local_path` to point at a local copy. We ran automated data-quality checks on 388 columns; 74 columns have at least one potential issue (50 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 12 columns with numeric values stored as text; 10 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 2 columns with inconsistent category casing; 2 columns that look like geographic coordinates). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 25 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In a pre-registered online experiment, participants completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism, and undertook a judgement bias task.

These translational tasks were originally developed for use with animals, on the basis of findings from human psychology that people with mood disorders, or in induced negative affective states, interpreted ambiguous words, phrases, facial expressions, and future scenarios more negatively (e.g. Eysenck et al., 1991; Joormann & Gotlib, 2006; Mathews et al., 1989; Park et al., 2016; Wright & Bower, 1992). In Harding et al.'s (2004) original animal judgement bias task, rats were trained to press a lever when they heard a tone associated with a food reward, and to refrain from pressing the lever when they heard a different tone to avoid a punishment (white noise).

Conversely, if the participant had similar reaction time profiles for both responses but responded 'pessimistically' more often, this would be reflected by a negative drift rate (with drift rate = 0 reflecting no drift towards either boundary) and suggest that the negative bias was generated during the decision-making process.

For example, Aylward et al. (2020) used a two-tone discrimination task in which participants had to press one key when a certain tone played to receive a high reward of £4 and had to press another key when a different tone played to receive a low reward of £1.
During testing, participants were also presented with an intermediate ambiguous tone on some trials, and their responses to this ambiguous tone were investigated.

In the task, participants had to decide whether to make the 'optimistic' response (the response associated with receiving a high reward) or the 'pessimistic' response (the response associated with receiving a low reward) when shown ambiguous visual stimuli.
Participants provided informed consent via an online consent form.
Participants were recruited and reimbursed for their time via Prolific (www.prolific.com).
The inclusion criteria were: (1) individuals over 18 years old, (2) individuals who currently lived in the UK, and (3) individuals who selected 'United Kingdom' as their nationality on Prolific.
To encourage engagement with the task, participants were told that they had a chance to earn the 20p bonus depending on whether they responded correctly on one trial selected at random.

To ensure that participants were attending to the possible trial outcomes, they were also told that for every 100 people that completed the task, the best performing participant would receive an extra bonus of £10.

We recruited 540 participants in total, based on a 93% completion rate observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al. (2022). 20 participants withdrew from the study, and data from a further 4 participants were excluded due to poor performance in the task (responding incorrectly on 50% or more of either of the unambiguous stimuli trials).

Participants completed the Generalised Anxiety Disorder Assessment (GAD-7) (Spitzer et al., 2006) to measure anxiety and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) (Kroenke et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2020) to measure depression.
All participants completed the study in a fixed order: consent form, judgement bias task (see below), LOT-R questionnaire, PHQ-8 questionnaire, GAD-7 questionnaire, demographics questionnaire.
Participants were instructed to ensure that they were sat upright, 60cm from the screen and that their screen was level.
To ensure that the stimuli appeared correctly, participants were required to calibrate their screen using Gorilla's screen calibration function.
Participants were told that the aim of the task was to earn as much money as possible.
Prior to each testing block, participants completed a training block of 20 trials using only the unambiguous stimuli.
During testing participants were also presented with ambiguous patches which were only slightly tilted to the left or right.
In addition, data from 4 participants were excluded due to poor performance in the task (responding incorrectly on 50% or more of either of the unambiguous stimuli trials).

Sex was a significant predictor of Optimistic Responses (LRT = 36.474, p < 0.001); post-hoc analysis revealed that male participants had significantly higher Optimistic Responses than females (male mean: 0.63, female mean: 0.56; z = 5.961, p < 0.001, Figure 4).

Sex was also a 490 significant predictor of drift rate (LRT = 31.364, p < 0.001); post-hoc analysis revealed that male 491 participants had significantly higher drift rates than females (z = 5.515, p < 0.001).

Using a large-scale preregistered online experiment where participants completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism, and undertook a judgement bias task, we confirmed that selfreported negative affect is associated with negative judgement biases during decision-making under ambiguity; individuals who reported higher anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-8) scores made a significantly lower proportion of 'optimistic' responses when faced with ambiguous stimuli in the judgement bias task.
Male participants were also significantly more 'optimistic' than females in the task, a finding not observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al.'s (2022) study.
A) Participants were required to classify Gabor patches as tilted to the left or right of vertical.
Each participant completed 240 trials in total with the four stimuli equally represented. n=516.

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 12 scripts: 9 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script could not be tried, because a file it needs was not downloaded**: Tidy_JB_task_data.R. It is not counted as a script that did not reproduce. The file: OE1 data and code/data_exp_34670-v8_task-y32s.csv (283 MB); files over 100 MB are not downloaded.

**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Trial_level_analysis.R", "Missing variable" = "Trial.Number", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "OE1 age and sex plots.R"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**13 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: Calculate_GAD7_score.R, Aim1_analysis.R, Tidy_demo_questionnaire_data.R, Aim2_analysis.R, Prep_data_for_HDDM.R, Calculate_PHQ8_score.R, Calculate_LOTRP_score.R, Plot_Prop_op.R, Process_HDDM_output.R.

text.text: Negative affect has been shown, in both humans and non-human animals, to bias decisionmaking under ambiguity away from so-called 'optimistic' responses that can yield higher rewards but also risk greater losses.

The judgement bias task, a cognitive task that uses ambiguous stimuli to measure such decisions as indicators of affective state, has successfully been translated from humans to animals and back again.
However, questions remain regarding how exactly affect influences 'optimistic' or 'pessimistic' decisions, and the extent to which dispositional pessimism also influences these decisions.
To further understand links between affect and decision-making, we carried out a judgement bias task in humans and measured self-reported affect and dispositional pessimism.
In a pre-registered online experiment, participants completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism, and undertook a judgement bias task.

Our results mirrored previous findings showing that selfreported negative affect is associated with negatively-biased decision-making under ambiguity; individuals who reported higher anxiety and depression made a significantly lower proportion of 'optimistic' responses to ambiguous stimuli in the judgement bias task.
However, we did not find sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis that self-reported dispositional pessimism is associated with 'pessimistic' responses in the task.

Drift-diffusion modelling revealed that the more negative (less 'optimistic') judgement bias associated with self-reported anxiety and depression, could be explained by a bias generated during the decision-making process, represented by a lower drift rate.
But due to high comorbidity, we were unable to determine whether negative judgement bias is driven primarily by anxiety or depression.
Affective states play an important role in guiding decision-making, especially when there is ambiguity surrounding the decision outcome (Loewenstein & Lerner, 2003; Mendl & Paul, 2020).
text.formatted: Affective states play an important role in guiding decision-making, especially when there is ambiguity surrounding the decision outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Loewenstein & Lerner, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mendl & Paul, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Judgement bias tasks capitalise on this relationship and have been successfully used to probe decision-making under ambiguity as an indicator of affective states in both human and nonhuman animals.

These translational tasks were originally developed for use with animals, on the basis of findings from human psychology that people with mood disorders, or in induced negative affective states, interpreted ambiguous words, phrases, facial expressions, and future scenarios more negatively (e.g. Eysenck et al., 1991; Joormann & Gotlib, 2006; Mathews et al., 1989; Park et al., 2016; Wright & Bower, 1992). In Harding et al.'s (2004) original animal judgement bias task, rats were trained to press a lever when they heard a tone associated with a food reward, and to refrain from pressing the lever when they heard a different tone to avoid a punishment (white noise).

text.text: Their responses to ambiguity were then tested by presenting tones of intermediate frequency.

Rats that had been housed in unpredictable conditions designed to induce a negative affective state were slower to make lever press responses to intermediate ambiguous tones, and tended to make fewer such responses, indicating a reduced anticipation of reward and hence a 'pessimistic'-like response to ambiguity.

Judgement bias tasks have now been used in over 200 studies as an indicator of animal affective state with results supporting the general hypothesis of an association between induced/presumed affective state and 'optimism' and 'pessimism' (see meta-analyses: Lagisz et al., 2020; Neville et al., 2020).

text.text: They have also been successfully back-translated for use with human populations (e.g. Anderson et al., 2012; Aylward et al., 2020; Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022; Iigaya et al., 2016; Neville et al., 2021a Neville et al., , 2021b;; Paul et al., 2011; Schick et al., 2013).

text.text: The human tasks can provide important insights into the processes underlying affective biases in judgements of ambiguity by using self-report as a marker of conscious affective experience.
In this study, we therefore investigate how self-reported negative affective states (anxiety and depression) are associated with biases in decision-making within the judgement bias task.
We also ask whether self-reported dispositional 'pessimism' plays a role in biasing decisions that may be separable from affective state per se.

Although judgement bias responses are typically described using the terms 'optimism ' and 'pessimism' (or 'optimistic-like' and 'pessimistic-like'), it is not clear to what extent dispositional pessimism might drive observed biases (Armbruster-Genç et al., 2024).

text.text: Previous research has investigated the influence of affective state, finding for example that individuals reporting negative affect (especially using clinically relevant measures of depression and anxiety) are more likely to show 'pessimistic' decision-making under ambiguity (Aylward et al., 2020; Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022).

text.text: However, according to Beck's cognitive model of depression (Beck et al., 1979), individuals with trait negative affect are more likely to have negative views about the future -i.e. increased pessimism -and therefore it is possible that predispositions to pessimistic thinking also influence decision-making under ambiguity.
text.formatted: However, according to Beck's cognitive model of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beck et al., 1979)</ref>, individuals with trait negative affect are more likely to have negative views about the future -i.e. increased pessimism -and therefore it is possible that predispositions to pessimistic thinking also influence decision-making under ambiguity.

text.text: Here we investigate this issue by measuring both affect and dispositional pessimism in humans performing a judgement bias task.

When referring to judgement bias task responses, we use the terms 'optimistic' and 'pessimistic' to maintain consistency with the literature, however they are used in an operational sense to describe task-specific response patterns rather than dispositional traits.

To analyse potential underlying processes, we employ computational modelling (see Neville et al., 2024), applying a drift-diffusion model (DDM: Ratcliff et al., 2016) which combines choice and reaction time data to provide insight into the mechanisms underlying the decision-process, typically in two-alternative forced choice tasks.
text.formatted: To analyse potential underlying processes, we employ computational modelling (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Neville et al., 2024)</ref>, applying a drift-diffusion model (DDM: <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Ratcliff et al., 2016)</ref> which combines choice and reaction time data to provide insight into the mechanisms underlying the decision-process, typically in two-alternative forced choice tasks.

text.text: The DDM conceptualises decisions as a process of evidence accumulation toward one of two decision thresholds, each representing an alternative choice.

Decisions are modelled as the rate of accumulation of evidence driving towards one or other threshold, combined with other parameters including whether the start point of the evidence accumulation process is closer to one of the thresholds.

One question which drift-diffusion modelling can be used to address is whether a bias towards one response is more likely to occur due to a pre-existing (start point) bias towards one option prior to stimulus presentation, or due to a difference in the rate of evidence accumulation (drift rate) during the decision-making process.
Consider data which show a negative judgement bias i.e. there is a higher proportion of 'pessimistic' responses than 'optimistic' responses.

If this was generated by an a priori bias, it would be reflected in a DDM by a relative start point parameter value of under 0.5 (with start point = 0.5 reflecting no a priori bias) due to the participant making the 'pessimistic' response more quickly and more often.

Conversely, if the participant had similar reaction time profiles for both responses but responded 'pessimistically' more often, this would be reflected by a negative drift rate (with drift rate = 0 reflecting no drift towards either boundary) and suggest that the negative bias was generated during the decision-making process.

It is possible to hypothesise that the influences of affective and dispositional pessimism on judgement bias may be related to a 'start point' bias within a DDM framework; both pessimistic individuals and those experiencing a negative mood state may be more likely to anticipate negative outcomes prior to stimulus presentation, and this would be reflected in a negatively biased start point.

However, there is some evidence from previous studies that negative affect is associated with a negative drift rate in human judgement bias task studies (Aylward et al., 2020; Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022), so we investigate this issue further here.

During testing, participants were also presented with an intermediate ambiguous tone on some trials, and their responses to this ambiguous tone were investigated.

Participants with mood or anxiety disorder symptoms made more 'pessimistic' responses, i.e. selected the key predicting the low reward indicating a negatively-biased anticipation of the smaller reward rather than the larger reward, compared to asymptomatic control participants. text.text: The GAD-7 and PHQ-8 questionnaires ask participants to report on symptoms occurring during the preceding two weeks, and we assumed that these provided a reliable metric of their general affective state when participating in the study.
We also assessed dispositional pessimism using the Revised Life Orientation Test (LOT-R: Scheier et al., 1994), as well as responses in a high/low reward active choice judgement bias task.

text.text: In the task, participants had to decide whether to make the 'optimistic' response (the response associated with receiving a high reward) or the 'pessimistic' response (the response associated with receiving a low reward) when shown ambiguous visual stimuli.

We hypothesised that there would be negative associations between each of the questionnaire measures (self-reported anxiety, depression, and dispositional pessimism) and 'optimistic' decision-making under ambiguity.

We also applied drift-diffusion modelling to investigate whether negative judgement biases were associated with a reduced start point parameter, indicating an a priori negative bias, and/or whether they were associated with a more negative drift-rate during the decision-making process itself.

text.text: Participants were recruited and reimbursed for their time via Prolific (www.prolific.com).

text.text: The inclusion criteria were: (1) individuals over 18 years old, (2) individuals who currently lived in the UK, and (3) individuals who selected 'United Kingdom' as their nationality on Prolific.
Data were collected in 11 batches between the 16th of July and the 10th of September 2021.
Prior to data collection, the whole experiment was piloted with 10 participants who were not included in the reported data set.
Participants who completed the study were paid £1.80 for their time plus a 20p bonus.
To encourage engagement with the task, participants were told that they had a chance to earn the 20p bonus depending on whether they responded correctly on one trial selected at random.
In fact, all participants received the 20p bonus regardless of performance.

To ensure that participants were attending to the possible trial outcomes, they were also told that for every 100 people that completed the task, the best performing participant would receive an extra bonus of £10.
This bonus was paid out accordingly.
To determine the target sample size, we used G*Power (v3.1.9.7, Faul et al., 2007) to conduct a power calculation.

text.text: The power calculation was based on a finding from a similar study (Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022), where a significant correlation of r=-0.13 was observed between the proportion of 'optimistic' responses to ambiguous stimuli in a decision-making task and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores.

Participants completed the Generalised Anxiety Disorder Assessment (GAD-7) (Spitzer et al., 2006) to measure anxiety and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) (Kroenke et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2020) to measure depression.

text.text: The GAD-7 and PHQ-8 were selected as they ask about how individuals have felt over the last two weeks which we used to indicate current negative affective states.
They are also clinically relevant, being routinely used as clinical measures of the severity of anxiety and depression symptoms in the UK (NHS England, 2025).

text.text: Participants also completed the Revised Life Orientation Test (LOT-R) (Scheier et al., 1994), a validated psychological tool used to measure individual differences in optimism and pessimism.

text.text: LOT-R scores were reverse coded to produce a pessimism (LOT-RP) score for each participant.
Participants' age in years, sex, and handedness were also recorded in a demographics questionnaire.
All participants completed the study in a fixed order: consent form, judgement bias task (see below), LOT-R questionnaire, PHQ-8 questionnaire, GAD-7 questionnaire, demographics questionnaire.
Participants were instructed to ensure that they were sat upright, 60cm from the screen and that their screen was level.
To ensure that the stimuli appeared correctly, participants were required to calibrate their screen using Gorilla's screen calibration function.

The stimuli used were symmetrical Gabor patches (10cm x 10cm, contrast: 50%, standard deviation of the Gaussian envelope: 1.5 degrees, grating spatial frequency: 0.5 cycles/degree) of various orientations, inspired by the stimuli used by Iigaya et al. (2016).
text.formatted: The stimuli used were symmetrical Gabor patches (10cm x 10cm, contrast: 50%, standard deviation of the Gaussian envelope: 1.5 degrees, grating spatial frequency: 0.5 cycles/degree) of various orientations, inspired by the stimuli used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Iigaya et al. (2016)</ref>.

text.text: The task required participants to classify the Gabor patches as tilted to the left or right of vertical by making keyboard press responses: 'Z' for left, 'M' for right (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The task required participants to classify the Gabor patches as tilted to the left or right of vertical by making keyboard press responses: 'Z' for left, 'M' for right (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: A trial was initiated by pressing the spacebar, after which a fixation cross was displayed in the centre of the screen for 500ms, followed by the stimulus for 250ms.
Participants could respond from the beginning of stimulus presentation and were instructed to respond "as quickly and as accurately as possible".
Feedback (£0, +£1, or +£4) was given immediately and displayed for 500ms.

The task used two unambiguous stimuli (-3.2 and 3.2 degrees from vertical) and two ambiguous stimuli (-0.05 and 0.05 degrees from vertical); the (un)ambiguity of these stimuli was previously validated by Iigaya et al. (2016).
text.formatted: The task used two unambiguous stimuli (-3.2 and 3.2 degrees from vertical) and two ambiguous stimuli (-0.05 and 0.05 degrees from vertical); the (un)ambiguity of these stimuli was previously validated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Iigaya et al. (2016)</ref>.

text.text: Correct responses were nominally rewarded with either a high reward (£4) or low reward (£1) depending on the Gabor patch orientation (left or right) and participants received £0 for an incorrect response.
Participants were told that the aim of the task was to earn as much money as possible.
The amount of 'money' won in the task determined which 6 participants received the £10 bonuses.

The high/low reward direction was counterbalanced within participants to account for any directional bias i.e. where a participant is predisposed to select either the left or right key, regardless of the stimulus.

Participants therefore completed two testing blocks, the first where left-tilted patches were nominally rewarded with £4 and the second where left-tilted patches were rewarded with £1 (and vice versa for right-tilted patches).
Both testing blocks consisted of 120 trials with all four stimuli equally represented across testing trials in a fixed random order.
Prior to each testing block, participants completed a training block of 20 trials using only the unambiguous stimuli.
Only data from the testing blocks were included in the analysis.
The key outcome of interest from the judgement bias task was the proportion of 'optimistic' responses to the ambiguous stimuli.
Here we define an 'optimistic' response as the response associated with the high-reward (£4) direction.

Responses to the two ambiguous stimuli (Ambiguous Negative and Ambiguous Positive) were compared using a paired-samples t-test, the assumptions of which were met; a Shapiro-Wilk test indicated that the difference scores did not deviate from normality (W = 0.998, p = 0.777) supported by visual inspection of the histogram and Q-Q plots.
A statistically significant difference was observed (t(515) = -2.15, p = 0.032) albeit with a very small effect size (mean difference = -0.008; Cohen's dz = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.18, -0.01]).

No significant difference in 'optimistic' responses between the Ambiguous Negative and Ambiguous Positive stimuli was found in post-hoc comparisons of our trial-level analysis (z = 2.496, p = 0.055; see supplementary material).

Based on this, and existing evidence that Gabor patch stimuli of these orientations cannot be reliably characterised above chance levels (Iigaya et al., 2016), the proportion of 'optimistic' responses were combined for both ambiguous stimuli to give each participant an 'Optimistic Response' score.

If they made the incorrect response they received £0.
During testing participants were also presented with ambiguous patches which were only slightly tilted to the left or right.
For ambiguous trials pressing 'Z' was classed as a 'pessimistic' response and pressing 'M' as an 'optimistic' response.

text.text: As per our preregistered plan, to determine whether demographic and questionnaire variables were significantly associated with the proportion of 'optimistic' responses to ambiguous stimuli in the judgement bias task (Optimistic Responses), we used a GLM containing the following independent variables: age, sex, anxiety score (from the GAD-7), depression score (from the PHQ-8) and pessimism score (from the LOT-RP).
Likelihood ratio tests were used to assess the significance of these variables.

To investigate the effects of sex on Optimistic Responses, posthoc comparisons were conducted using a simultaneous pairwise Tukey procedure for general linear hypotheses with the R package 'multcomp' (Hothorn et al., 2008).
text.formatted: To investigate the effects of sex on Optimistic Responses, posthoc comparisons were conducted using a simultaneous pairwise Tukey procedure for general linear hypotheses with the R package 'multcomp' <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hothorn et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In our preregistration we also anticipated that the three questionnaire scores would be highly correlated and therefore would require separate GLMs to independently test for associations between each questionnaire score and Optimistic Responses.
Pearson's correlations were used to assess the association between the three questionnaire scores.
As these were highly correlated with each other as expected, we ran the three further GLMs, each containing one of the questionnaires as well as age and sex.
Model fit was compared using Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).

The Optimistic Responses summary score was used to make our analysis comparable to 'standard' analyses of human and animal judgement bias tasks, however recognising the loss of information with this approach, additional trial-level analyses were performed to check whether similar results were observed from the complete dataset (see supplementary material).

To investigate how negative affect influences the decision-making process at the individual level, drift-diffusion modelling (DDM) was applied to the judgement bias task data using the Python toolbox HDDM (version 1.0.1 with Python 3.9.13, Wiecki et al., 2013).
text.formatted: To investigate how negative affect influences the decision-making process at the individual level, drift-diffusion modelling (DDM) was applied to the judgement bias task data using the Python toolbox HDDM (version 1.0.1 with Python 3.9.13, <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Wiecki et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Only data for the ambiguous judgement bias task trials were included in the model.

The model was fitted hierarchically using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling and contained 4 parameters: drift rate (v), threshold separation (a), start point bias (z), and non-decision time (t).
We ran 10,000 MCMC iterations, discarding the first 500 samples as burn-in.
Starting values were optimised prior to sampling to facilitate convergence.
Model convergence was assessed through visual inspection of trace plots and autocorrelation functions.
These diagnostics indicated stable post-burn-in sampling, good mixing, and no evidence of systematic trends.
In addition, posterior predictive checks indicated that the fitted model adequately reproduced the observed reaction time distributions, suggesting satisfactory convergence and model fit.
Parameter recovery checks showed good recovery, and a hold-out validation procedure confirmed good predictive performance for held-out data (see supplementary material for details).
DDM parameters were estimated using a fully hierarchical Bayesian model implemented in HDDM, such that individual estimates were regularised by group-level priors.

Although HDDM allows covariates to be included directly, initial analysis revealed that anxiety, depression, and pessimism questionnaire scores were correlated, making their simultaneous inclusion prone to multicollinearity and reduced identifiability.
Instead, relationships between DDM parameters and demographic and questionnaire variables were subsequently examined in separate general linear models (GLMs).

For each DDM parameter we ran a GLM containing age and sex, and three further GLMs containing age, sex, and one of the questionnaire scores: anxiety (GAD-7) score, depression (PHQ-8) score, or pessimism (LOT-RP) score.
For each DDM parameter, the model with the best fit was selected using the lowest AIC value and results for this model only are reported.

To investigate the effects of sex on the DDM parameter estimates, post-hoc comparisons were conducted using a simultaneous pairwise Tukey procedure for general linear hypotheses with the R package 'multcomp' (Hothorn et al., 2008).

We conducted a human judgement bias study to investigate how self-reported affect and dispositional pessimism may bias decision-making under ambiguity.

Using a large-scale preregistered online experiment where participants completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism, and undertook a judgement bias task, we confirmed that selfreported negative affect is associated with negative judgement biases during decision-making under ambiguity; individuals who reported higher anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-8) scores made a significantly lower proportion of 'optimistic' responses when faced with ambiguous stimuli in the judgement bias task.

This is consistent with previous findings in the literature (e.g. Aylward et al., 2020; Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022), despite differences in the judgement bias tasks and questionnaires used, suggesting that the association between negative affect and 'pessimistic' decision-making under ambiguity is robust and generalised.
text.formatted: This is consistent with previous findings in the literature (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aylward et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022)</ref>, despite differences in the judgement bias tasks and questionnaires used, suggesting that the association between negative affect and 'pessimistic' decision-making under ambiguity is robust and generalised.

text.text: This result is also consistent with translational judgement bias studies conducted with nonhuman animals, where animals presumed to be in more negative affective states tend to show negative (less 'optimistic') biases in judgement bias tasks (Lagisz et al., 2020; Neville et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This result is also consistent with translational judgement bias studies conducted with nonhuman animals, where animals presumed to be in more negative affective states tend to show negative (less 'optimistic') biases in judgement bias tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lagisz et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Neville et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We also showed that while self-reported dispositional pessimism (LOT-RP) scores are significantly positively correlated with both anxiety and depression scores, we did not find sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis that self-reported pessimism is inversely associated with 'optimistic' responses in the judgement bias task.
This is contrary to our original hypothesis and suggests that the LOT-R questionnaire and the judgement bias task may be capturing different components or constructs of affect.
A recent study by Armbruster-Genç et al. (2024) also found no significant correlation between LOT-R scores and judgement bias task responses.
text.formatted: A recent study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Armbruster-Genç et al. (2024)</ref> also found no significant correlation between LOT-R scores and judgement bias task responses.

text.text: If we take the LOT-R questionnaire as a gold standard measure of dispositional optimism (or inversely, pessimism), these findings call into question whether judgement bias task responses should be referred to as 'optimistic' or 'pessimistic', or whether a change in terminology would be more accurate, such as 'positively biased' and 'negatively biased' responses.

This is particularly relevant for experiments involving non-human animals where individuals are often classified as being 'optimistic' or 'pessimistic' based on judgement bias task outputs (e.g. Espigares et al., 2022; Lecorps et al., 2018; Papciak et al., 2013; Rygula et al., 2012); although such terms can be defined operationally (e.g. Matheson et al., 2008), their use may misleadingly imply human-like constructs.
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant for experiments involving non-human animals where individuals are often classified as being 'optimistic' or 'pessimistic' based on judgement bias task outputs (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Espigares et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lecorps et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Papciak et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Rygula et al., 2012)</ref>; although such terms can be defined operationally (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Matheson et al., 2008)</ref>, their use may misleadingly imply human-like constructs.

text.text: In the present paper, we continue to use the terms 'optimistic' and 'pessimistic' to remain consistent with the wider literature, however they are used operationally to describe task responses rather than broader personality traits.
Computational modelling of decision-making data allows us to gain a richer understanding of how affect could be influencing underlying decision-making processes.

Here, we used the driftdiffusion model (Ratcliff et al., 2016) to understand the potential cognitive mechanisms underlying the bias towards the 'pessimistic' response or away from the 'optimistic' response observed in those with higher anxiety and depression scores.

text.text: All drift-diffusion model analyses were not preregistered meaning any findings are exploratory and should be interpreted cautiously.

Despite our theory-based prediction that individuals reporting higher anxiety and depression scores would have a pre-existing bias towards making the 'pessimistic' response to ambiguous stimuli (Beck et al., 1979), the results suggest that the negative bias emerged during the decision-making process rather than a priori; anxiety scores were significantly associated with a decreased drift rate but not with a change in start point bias.

text.text: In fact, the proportion of 'optimistic' responses to ambiguous stimuli and drift rate were highly and significantly correlated.
This is consistent with previous findings in humans (Aylward et al., 2020; Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022) and rats (Hales et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This is consistent with previous findings in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Aylward et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022)</ref> and rats <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hales et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We also found a marginal positive association between depression scores and threshold separation values, a parameter which represents how much information is required to reach a decision.
In previous human judgement bias studies, no relationship between negative affect and threshold separation has been observed (Aylward et al., 2020; Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In previous human judgement bias studies, no relationship between negative affect and threshold separation has been observed <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Aylward et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, rats showing a negative bias (induced by a pharmacological manipulation or chronic stress) have also been found to have an increased threshold separation compared to controls (Hales et al., 2016).
text.formatted: However, rats showing a negative bias (induced by a pharmacological manipulation or chronic stress) have also been found to have an increased threshold separation compared to controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hales et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, studies using different decision-making tasks to investigate mood disorders have also identified a relationship between more negative affect and increased threshold separation values using drift-diffusion modelling (Edgar et al., 2025; Lawlor et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Similarly, studies using different decision-making tasks to investigate mood disorders have also identified a relationship between more negative affect and increased threshold separation values using drift-diffusion modelling <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Edgar et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lawlor et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This could potentially reflect more cautious decision-making with increased depression severity.
It is important to note that many other tasks have been developed to explore affective biases in decision-making.

For example, the judgement bias task used here shares similarities with the probabilistic reward task (PRT) developed by Pizzagalli and colleagues, which has been widely used to study anhedonia and depression (Pizzagalli et al., 2008a; Pizzagalli et al., 2008b).
text.formatted: For example, the judgement bias task used here shares similarities with the probabilistic reward task (PRT) developed by Pizzagalli and colleagues, which has been widely used to study anhedonia and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pizzagalli et al., 2008a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pizzagalli et al., 2008b)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to our high/low reward design, the PRT uses two stimuli reinforced with equal reward magnitude but differing probabilities, such that correct identification of one ('rich') stimulus is rewarded more frequently than the other ('lean') stimulus, leading healthy participants to develop a response bias towards the rich stimulus; this bias is typically reduced in individuals with anhedonia and depression (Pizzagalli et al., 2008a; Pizzagalli et al., 2008b).
text.formatted: In contrast to our high/low reward design, the PRT uses two stimuli reinforced with equal reward magnitude but differing probabilities, such that correct identification of one ('rich') stimulus is rewarded more frequently than the other ('lean') stimulus, leading healthy participants to develop a response bias towards the rich stimulus; this bias is typically reduced in individuals with anhedonia and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pizzagalli et al., 2008a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pizzagalli et al., 2008b)</ref>.

text.text: Drift-diffusion modelling of PRT performance has shown that this reduced response bias is associated with both reduced drift rate and reduced starting point bias (Shen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Drift-diffusion modelling of PRT performance has shown that this reduced response bias is associated with both reduced drift rate and reduced starting point bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Shen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to judgement bias tasks, which rely on explicitly learned reward contingencies before testing responses to ambiguity, the PRT captures the gradual development of a response bias under uncertainty, requiring participants to learn reward probabilities over time (Pizzagalli et al., 2008a; Pizzagalli et al., 2008b).
text.formatted: In contrast to judgement bias tasks, which rely on explicitly learned reward contingencies before testing responses to ambiguity, the PRT captures the gradual development of a response bias under uncertainty, requiring participants to learn reward probabilities over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pizzagalli et al., 2008a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pizzagalli et al., 2008b)</ref>.

text.text: While some PRT studies link negative affect to altered learning rate, there is evidence to suggest that these effects instead reflect reduced reward sensitivity (Huys et al., 2013).
text.formatted: While some PRT studies link negative affect to altered learning rate, there is evidence to suggest that these effects instead reflect reduced reward sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Huys et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In this case, the observed effects of negative affect on decision-making in both tasks may be driven by overlapping underlying mechanisms.
The use of multiple complementary tasks such as these in the same participants, coupled with computational modelling of the data, would be beneficial in further characterising affective biases.
A secondary aim of this study was to explore whether anxiety or depression symptoms drive 'pessimistic' decision-making in the judgement bias task.
We found anxiety and depression scores to be very highly correlated.
This meant that they could not be included in the same model, and when considered separately, both anxiety and depression scores were significantly associated with a negative judgement bias.
Given the high multicollinearity between anxiety and depression measures, it is not possible to determine which is the primary driver of our observed results.
Accordingly, we suggest that the findings indicate negative affect more broadly influences 'pessimistic' decision-making under ambiguity.
When analysed separately, anxiety and depression scores were also both significantly associated with a lower drift rate.
Again, we observed only a small difference in model fit, so conclude that the lower drift rate is associated with negative affect, rather than anxiety or depression specifically.

Daniel-Watanabe et al.'s (2022) study found that depression scores, measured using the Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI: Beck et al., 1996), were more strongly related to judgement bias task performance than anxiety scores, measured using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI: Spielberger et al., 1983).
text.formatted: Daniel-Watanabe et al.'s (2022) study found that depression scores, measured using the Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI: <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Beck et al., 1996)</ref>, were more strongly related to judgement bias task performance than anxiety scores, measured using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI: <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Spielberger et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: However, their exploratory factor analysis suggested that depression and anxiety scores should be combined into a single latent factor.
Due to high comorbidity of anxiety and depression, other studies have also combined anxiety and depression (e.g. Aylward et al. (2020) compared a mood disorder group to a control group).
text.formatted: Due to high comorbidity of anxiety and depression, other studies have also combined anxiety and depression (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aylward et al. (2020)</ref> compared a mood disorder group to a control group).

text.text: Whilst it is possible that negative judgement bias is driven by a negative trait factor common to both anxiety and depression, future research could use more specific questionnaires, such as measures based on the tripartite model (e.g. the Mood and Anxiety Symptom Questionnaire; MASQ; Watson et al., 1995), to better dissociate anxiety and depression symptoms and explore whether particular symptoms or sets of symptoms are more strongly associated with judgement bias.
text.formatted: Whilst it is possible that negative judgement bias is driven by a negative trait factor common to both anxiety and depression, future research could use more specific questionnaires, such as measures based on the tripartite model (e.g. the Mood and Anxiety Symptom Questionnaire; MASQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Watson et al., 1995)</ref>, to better dissociate anxiety and depression symptoms and explore whether particular symptoms or sets of symptoms are more strongly associated with judgement bias.

text.text: Studies such as ours which have used an individual differences approach by sampling from the general population have also found very small effect sizes (e.g. Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022; Armbruster-Genç et al., 2024) compared to studies which have compared patient and control groups (e.g. Aylward et al., 2020), potentially suggesting that the observed negative bias may be best characterised as a clinical mood disorder symptom; using symptom score cutoffs (GAD-7 ≥ 10; PHQ-8 ≥ 10) only 21% of participants in our study would be classed as having moderate to severe anxiety and 26% as having moderate to severe depression (Spitzer et al., 2006; Kroenke et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Studies such as ours which have used an individual differences approach by sampling from the general population have also found very small effect sizes (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Armbruster-Genç et al., 2024)</ref> compared to studies which have compared patient and control groups (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aylward et al., 2020)</ref>, potentially suggesting that the observed negative bias may be best characterised as a clinical mood disorder symptom; using symptom score cutoffs (GAD-7 ≥ 10; PHQ-8 ≥ 10) only 21% of participants in our study would be classed as having moderate to severe anxiety and 26% as having moderate to severe depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Spitzer et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kroenke et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wu et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This may also help to explain why the normally distributed responses we received to the LOT-RP pessimism questionnaire were not significantly related to judgement bias task responses.

One concern highlighted by the small effect sizes observed here and in other human judgement bias studies (e.g. Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022; Armbruster-Genç et al., 2024), is how sensitive and selective these tasks are to detecting and measuring negative (or positive) affect.
text.formatted: One concern highlighted by the small effect sizes observed here and in other human judgement bias studies (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Armbruster-Genç et al., 2024)</ref>, is how sensitive and selective these tasks are to detecting and measuring negative (or positive) affect.

text.text: Currently it is unclear whether small or null effects in these studies reflect limited sensitivity or specificity of the judgement bias tasks themselves, limitations of the self-report measures used to capture affect, or both.

These human back-translated judgement bias task studies are relatively new therefore further work is needed to disentangle these possibilities and evaluate their reliability and validity for translational research (Pike et al., 2021).
text.formatted: These human back-translated judgement bias task studies are relatively new therefore further work is needed to disentangle these possibilities and evaluate their reliability and validity for translational research <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Pike et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: If the relationship between affect and judgement bias is genuinely weak, even in humans who can explicitly report their affective state (albeit imperfectly), this necessarily limits how strongly judgement bias outcomes can be interpreted in animals, where affect must be inferred indirectly.
In addition, animal studies are likely to be underpowered, particularly when weaker affect manipulations are used, as it is difficult to achieve large enough sample sizes to detect small effects.

Importantly, however, meta-analyses of animal judgement bias studies indicate that both pharmacological and non-pharmacological affect manipulations produce small to small-to-moderate effects in the predicted direction (Lagisz et al., 2020; Neville et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Importantly, however, meta-analyses of animal judgement bias studies indicate that both pharmacological and non-pharmacological affect manipulations produce small to small-to-moderate effects in the predicted direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lagisz et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Neville et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that judgement bias is sensitive to affective manipulations, but potentially with limited precision, reinforcing the need to interpret it as one component within a broader framework of cognitive, behavioural, and physiological measures of affect.
It is also important to consider that responses in judgement bias tasks may be influenced by other factors and to measure and control for these where possible.

When piloting the task, we found that many participants showed a directional bias towards one of the two decision keys (Z or M), which we addressed by using within subject counterbalancing by swapping the high/low reward direction halfway through the task.
We also found significant effects of age and sex on judgement bias.
Consistent with Daniel-Watanabe et al.'s, (2022) study, the proportion of 'optimistic' responses made to ambiguous stimuli in the task significantly decreased with age.
Male participants were also significantly more 'optimistic' than females in the task, a finding not observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al.'s (2022) study.

Whilst these age and sex effects are interesting, they were not a focus of the study and were not preregistered therefore they should be treated as exploratory findings that warrant further investigation, especially as the existing literature on this topic is limited.

It is also likely that judgement bias tasks are capturing other non-affect related traits, such as risk-taking behaviour which has been shown to be higher in males than females (e.g. Byrnes et al., 1999; Charness & Gneezy, 2012).
text.formatted: It is also likely that judgement bias tasks are capturing other non-affect related traits, such as risk-taking behaviour which has been shown to be higher in males than females (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Byrnes et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Charness & Gneezy, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Due to time constraints, we did not include an IQ measure, however previous work suggests that IQ has a significant effect on these types of tasks where logic may to some extent override emotional biases (Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Due to time constraints, we did not include an IQ measure, however previous work suggests that IQ has a significant effect on these types of tasks where logic may to some extent override emotional biases <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, the types of reinforcers used within the judgement bias task are likely to influence responses.

For example, we might predict that tasks which use high versus low rewards would be more sensitive to changes in reward processing and therefore more relevant to depression symptoms (Whitton et al., 2015) whereas a task using a reward versus punishment design may be more sensitive to changes in punishment processing and therefore more relevant to anxiety symptoms (Robinson et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, we might predict that tasks which use high versus low rewards would be more sensitive to changes in reward processing and therefore more relevant to depression symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Whitton et al., 2015)</ref> whereas a task using a reward versus punishment design may be more sensitive to changes in punishment processing and therefore more relevant to anxiety symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Robinson et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: While our study focused on the relationship between self-reported anxiety and depression during the past two weeks and judgement bias performance, responses may also have been influenced by shorter-term changes in participants' affective states (Loewenstein & Lerner, 2003).
text.formatted: While our study focused on the relationship between self-reported anxiety and depression during the past two weeks and judgement bias performance, responses may also have been influenced by shorter-term changes in participants' affective states <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Loewenstein & Lerner, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Over the short test session, we expected that participants' moods would be relatively stable and therefore would predictably influence task and questionnaire responses over the whole session.
However, due to the fixed study order it is possible that task performance could have influenced subsequent questionnaire responses.
For example, poorer performance on the judgement bias task may have induced a temporarily more negative mood, potentially inflating self-reported symptoms of anxiety or depression.

A fixed study order was used to facilitate the investigation of individual differences, and the judgement bias task was completed first as we believed it likely that explicitly directing participants' attention to their affective state during self-report could attenuate the extent to which affect influenced decision-making in the judgement bias task (Kassam & Mendes, 2013).
text.formatted: A fixed study order was used to facilitate the investigation of individual differences, and the judgement bias task was completed first as we believed it likely that explicitly directing participants' attention to their affective state during self-report could attenuate the extent to which affect influenced decision-making in the judgement bias task <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kassam & Mendes, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, completing questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism may induce a negative affective state which could influence task performance.
Nonetheless, potential order effects should be considered when interpreting our findings.

Shorter-term (event-triggered) emotions may last only seconds to minutes and are also likely to vary over a test-session, particularly in response to trial feedback e.g. winning £4 may induce a positively-valenced emotion which could positively bias decision-making on a subsequent trial (Neville et al., 2021a).
text.formatted: Shorter-term (event-triggered) emotions may last only seconds to minutes and are also likely to vary over a test-session, particularly in response to trial feedback e.g. winning £4 may induce a positively-valenced emotion which could positively bias decision-making on a subsequent trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Neville et al., 2021a)</ref>.

text.text: Future experiments could include self-reported measures of both current mood and short-term emotion to differentiate between their effects on judgement bias task responses; a questionnaire to assess immediate mood (e.g. the Profile of Mood States (POMS) questionnaire (Grove & Prapavessis, 1992)) could be included alongside the anxiety and depression questionnaires used in this study and moment -to-moment affective states could also be assessed using the addition of affect grids throughout the task which allow participants to report on their current affective valence and arousal (Neville et al., 2021a (Neville et al., , 2021b)).
text.formatted: Future experiments could include self-reported measures of both current mood and short-term emotion to differentiate between their effects on judgement bias task responses; a questionnaire to assess immediate mood (e.g. the Profile of Mood States (POMS) questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Grove & Prapavessis, 1992)</ref>) could be included alongside the anxiety and depression questionnaires used in this study and moment -to-moment affective states could also be assessed using the addition of affect grids throughout the task which allow participants to report on their current affective valence and arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Neville et al., 2021a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Neville et al., , 2021b))</ref>.

text.text: In addition to affective states influencing task responses, it is likely that affective states also influenced how participants responded to the questionnaires which we used to capture negative affect over the past two weeks.

To ensure that the questionnaires used here are capturing longerlasting affect, the experiment could be repeated with the same individuals over multiple timepoints to check the stability of both questionnaire and judgement bias task responses.
In conclusion, we confirmed that self-reported negative affect is associated with negatively biased decision-making under ambiguity in humans, supporting the generality of this finding.
We also found that this negative bias appears to arise during the decision-making process as opposed to being a result of an a priori bias towards making the 'pessimistic' response.

However, contrary to our hypothesis, our results did not provide sufficient evidence for an association between self-reported dispositional pessimism and 'pessimistic' responses in the judgement bias task.

Due to a strong significant correlation between self-reported anxiety and depression symptoms it was not possible to definitively disentangle the respective effects of anxiety and depression on judgement bias task responses.
